catalog_quote: All members of the two open lexical classes, nouns and verbs, have one main stress, which falls on the final syllable of the word if this syllable contains a long vowel; otherwise stress is on the penultimate syllable. In general, secondary stress will fall on alternate syllables counting back from the antepenultimate, e.g malamake ... 'morning'; but the internal structure of the word may influence secondary stress assignment, in that lexical roots and some affixes retain their own stress pattern in morphologically complex forms, e.g. hakamemea ... 'be pregnant' (haka- 'CAUS'+memea 'child'). ... [p.26] In Vaeakau-Taumako, this opposition is contrastive mainly in word-final syllables. Short final vowels are always unstressed, and in some cases devoiced or dropped (cf. 2.2 above). audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages and the exception passage are verbatim in the held De Gruyter preview PDF at the stated locators (§2.2 p.23; §2.3.1.2 pp.26-28). (2) Deciding source is the 2011 Mouton Grammar Library reference grammar (499 pp) by the language's documenters, the top item in Glottolog's descriptive list; Crossref and Semantic Scholar searches show no phonology article, instrumental study, JIPA illustration or dissertation on Vaeakau-Taumako/Pileni prosody, so nothing better exists. (3) The classification 'weight (final CVV else penult), right edge, alternating secondary stress, listed exceptions (antepenult shift with single-vowel penult)' matches the source's primary formulation; the source itself notes the equivalent VV=uniform-penult analysis, which our the primary-stress rule already records.
